bibliography.abstract: Abstract Micro, Small, and Medium-Sized Enterprises (MSMEs) contribute approximately 25% of Bangladesh’s GDP and account for nearly 80% of employment. However, the influence of intra-urban mobility on the residential and workplace decisions of small business owners and employees remains underexplored. Existing studies have focused largely on general commuting behavior, with limited attention to the interaction between business location, residential choice, and mobility dynamics within Dhaka’s commercial centers. This study examines the mobility patterns and socio-economic characteristics of small business owners and employees in Gulistan and Gulshan commercial areas. A mixed-methods approach was adopted using questionnaire data from 384 respondents, analyzed through descriptive statistics, multiple regression, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and geospatial techniques using SPSS, MS Excel, and ArcGIS. The results show that workers in Gulshan exhibit higher educational attainment, greater residential stability, shorter commuting distances, and more efficient mobility than those in Gulistan, where longer commutes, higher transport costs, and greater residential and occupational mobility prevail. PCA extracted five principal components explaining 92% of the total variance, while the classification model achieved 94% accuracy, confirming clear structural differences between the two commercial areas. Regression analysis identified sex (p < 0.10) and commuting distance (p < 0.01) as the significant predictors of commuting time. The findings support integrated land-use and transport planning through mixed-use development, improved public transport, enhanced pedestrian infrastructure, and gender-responsive mobility policies to promote equitable and sustainable urban development in Dhaka.

en.caveats: The findings are based on a relatively small sample of 384 survey respondents across only two commercial districts in Dhaka, which may limit generalizability to other commercial areas in the city.
en.what: This study analyzed the mobility patterns and socio-economic characteristics of 384 small business owners and employees in Dhaka's Gulistan and Gulshan commercial areas using descriptive statistics, multiple regression, and Principal Component Analysis. The analysis revealed that workers in Gulshan experience shorter commutes, lower residential mobility, and higher educational attainment compared to those in Gulistan, who face longer travel distances and higher transport costs. Regression modeling identified gender and commuting distance as the primary predictors of commuting time, while a classification model distinguished the structural differences between the two commercial zones with 94% accuracy.
en.why: It provides empirical evidence of how intra-urban mobility constraints and residential choices differ sharply between formal and informal commercial hubs within the same city, establishing a baseline for gender-responsive transport and mixed-use zoning policies.
